content.text: The United Kingdom (UK) is made up of four countries: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

thumbnail.altText: Map of the UK showing the four countries

content.title: Each country has its own capital city:

content.text: Other major cities include Manchester, Birmingham, Liverpool, Leeds, Bristol, Glasgow, Aberdeen, Swansea and Newport.
The UK is an island nation located off the northwestern coast of Europe. The mainland is about 870 miles (1,400 km) from north to south with a population of approximately 67.6 million people.
English is the main language spoken in the UK. Welsh is spoken in Wales, Gaelic in parts of Scotland and Irish Gaelic in parts of Northern Ireland.

thumbnail.altText: Different languages spoken in the UK

content.text: You will hear many different accents and dialects across the UK. Learning English is essential for settling into life in the UK.
Spring (March-May): Often rainy, with flowers and trees blooming. Days start getting longer and warmer.
Summer (June-August): The warmest season with long sunny days and occasional thunderstorms.
Autumn (September-November): Days get colder, leaves fall from trees, and it can be wet and windy.
Winter (December-February): The coldest season with freezing temperatures, ice and sometimes snow. You will need warm clothing - layers, a thick coat, scarf, hat and gloves.
Daylight savings: Clocks go forward one hour in March and back one hour in October.

The UK has public holidays called Bank Holidays when banks and many businesses are closed. Key holidays include New Year’s Day, Early May Bank Holiday, August Bank Holiday, Christmas Day and Boxing Day.
Each of the four countries may also have its own holidays, such as St. Andrew’s Day in Scotland.
The UK is a constitutional monarchy and a parliamentary democracy. Tap each dot to learn more.

interactiveDots.title: Head of State
interactiveDots.text: The Head of State is King Charles III. The monarch’s role is largely ceremonial.

interactiveDots.title: Prime Minister
interactiveDots.text: The Prime Minister leads the government. Kier Starmer is the current Prime Minister. Members of Parliament (MPs) are elected by citizens to represent them.

interactiveDots.title: Parliament
interactiveDots.text: Parliament has three parts: the King, the House of Lords and the House of Commons. Elections must be held at least every five years.

interactiveDots.title: The Union Jack
interactiveDots.text: The UK flag is called the Union Jack. It combines the crosses of Saint George (England), Saint Andrew (Scotland) and Saint Patrick (Ireland).

content.text: Britain is a multicultural, diverse society, especially in larger towns and cities.
British values include tolerance (respect for everyone), fairness (treating people equally) and respect (for different views, religions and ways of life).
Men and women are treated equally. You are expected to be tolerant and respectful of others.
The official religion is Christianity, but the UK is a multi-faith society. You are free to practise your religion.
Many towns and cities have mosques, churches, synagogues, temples and other places of worship. People of all faiths and no faith respect each other’s beliefs.

thumbnail.altText: Places of worship in the UK

content.text: British social etiquette may be different from what you are used to. Tap each dot to learn the key dos and don’ts.

interactiveDots.title: Queuing
interactiveDots.text: Always queue (wait in line) and wait your turn. Pushing in is considered very rude.

interactiveDots.title: Politeness
interactiveDots.text: Say “please”, “thank you” and “sorry” frequently. Be on time for appointments.

interactiveDots.title: Public Transport
interactiveDots.text: Give up your seat for pregnant women, elderly people or disabled people.

interactiveDots.title: Things to Avoid
interactiveDots.text: Do not spit in public, smoke in enclosed public places, speak too loudly or throw litter on the ground.

content.text: he official currency is the British Pound (£), also called Pound Sterling. Coins come in: 1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, £1 and £2.
Notes come in: £5, £10, £20 and £50. One pound (£1) equals 100 pence (100p).
For example, five 20p coins make £1, and ten 10p coins make £1.

content.text: Your journey to the UK will be arranged by staff from the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
IOM staff will guide you through every step of the travel process. You will not be travelling alone.
You should think carefully about what to pack. Tap each dot to find out what to bring and what to leave behind.

interactiveDots.title: Clothes
interactiveDots.text: Pack comfortable clothes for travelling and warm clothes for UK weather - a coat, hat, scarf and gloves.

interactiveDots.title: Documents and Medication
interactiveDots.text: Keep important documents in your hand luggage. Bring prescription medication with a doctor’s letter explaining what it is.

interactiveDots.title: Personal Items
interactiveDots.text: Bring a small amount of money and items with sentimental value such as photos or small keepsakes. If you have a baby, bring nappies, formula, bottles and a change of clothes.

interactiveDots.title: Do NOT Pack
interactiveDots.text: Do not pack knives, scissors, sharp objects, weapons, liquids over 100ml in hand luggage, illegal drugs, or large amounts of cash without declaring it.

interactiveDots.title: Luggage Allowance
interactiveDots.text: Each passenger is usually allowed one or two checked bags (approximately 23kg each) and one carry-on bag. Check your specific allowance with IOM staff.

content.text: You will receive an IOM bag on your travel day. This bag is very important. It contains your travel documents, your Skills Profile, medical documents and important paperwork for UK immigration.
Always keep the IOM bag with you as your hand luggage. Never put it in checked luggage. You will need to hand it to immigration officials when you arrive in the UK.
Check-in: You will check in your luggage and receive your boarding pass. This shows your seat number and gate number.
Security screening: You and your bags will be scanned. This is normal and happens to everyone. You may need to remove belts, shoes, jackets and electronic items.
Passport control: Your travel documents will be checked. Answer any questions calmly and honestly.
Departure gate: Wait at your assigned gate until boarding is announced. Make sure you have your IOM travel bag and boarding pass ready.
When you board the plane, find your seat using the number on your boarding pass. Tap each dot to learn about life on the plane.

thumbnail.altText: Illustration of the inside of an aeroplane with tappable dot areas

interactiveDots.title: Seat Belts
interactiveDots.text: You must fasten your seat belt during take-off and landing, and at any other time when the seat belt sign is switched on or when instructed by the cabin crew.

interactiveDots.title: No Smoking
interactiveDots.text: You cannot smoke on the plane. This includes e-cigarettes.

interactiveDots.title: Food and Drink
interactiveDots.text: Food and drinks will be provided during the flight. If you have dietary requirements (e.g. halal, vegetarian, allergies), let IOM staff know before the journey. Alcohol may be offered you are not required to drink it.

interactiveDots.title: Using the Toilet
interactiveDots.text: Aeroplane toilets are small. Look for the “Vacant” and “Occupied” signs on the door. Lock the door when inside, this turns on the light. Only put toilet paper in the toilet. If unsure, ask the cabin crew for help.

interactiveDots.title: Safety
interactiveDots.text: Follow the safety demonstration from the cabin crew. Put your seat upright and tray table away during take-off and landing. Store your carry-on bag in the overhead compartment or under the seat in front of you.

content.text: Some flights may have a transit stop - a stopover in another country. If this happens, stay in the transit area of the airport. Do NOT leave the airport or go through immigration.
Follow IOM staff instructions and always keep your IOM travel bag and documents with you. If you are unsure what to do, ask airport staff for help.

When you arrive in the UK, you will go through UK immigration (border control). Show your travel documents from the IOM travel bag. Immigration officers may ask you questions, answer calmly and honestly.
After passing through immigration, collect your checked luggage from the baggage claim area.
Someone will be waiting to meet you after you collect your luggage. They will take you to your accommodation. You will not have to pay for transport.
Keep your IOM travel bag with you at all times - never put it in checked luggage. Keep your family together throughout the journey.
If you feel unwell, tell IOM staff or cabin crew immediately. Take any medication you need in your hand luggage.
If you get lost or separated, ask airport staff for help. Stay calm, the journey may feel long, but people are there to help you.

units.title: YOUR FIRST FEW WEEKS IN THE UK

thumbnail.altText: Your First Few Weeks in the UK

content.text: When you arrive in the UK, you will have the legal right to stay. Tap each dot to learn more.

interactiveDots.title: Your Rights
interactiveDots.text: You can access public services such as healthcare and schools. You have the right to work from your first day. You can apply for benefits to cover your basic living costs. You can apply for British citizenship in the future.

interactiveDots.title: Your eVisa
interactiveDots.text: You will be supported to access your eVisa through an online UKVI account set up by the UK Home Office. Every family member receives an eVisa, including children and babies. It is free of charge.

interactiveDots.title: Why Your eVisa Matters
interactiveDots.text: Your eVisa is evidence of your identity and legal status. You need it to access benefits, the NHS and other services. Unlike a physical document, it cannot be lost, damaged or stolen. Keep your UKVI account access safe and secure.

content.text: When you arrive, you will have support to help you settle in. Someone will meet you at the airport and take you to your accommodation. Tap each dot to learn what your support network will help you with.

interactiveDots.title: Your Home
interactiveDots.text: Settle into your accommodation. If your flight arrives late, you may be accommodated overnight with food and drinks provided.

interactiveDots.title: Essential Registration
interactiveDots.text: Access your eVisa, open a bank account, register with a local GP (doctor) and dentist, and register children at local schools.

interactiveDots.title: Money and Benefits
interactiveDots.text: Understand UK money and how to budget. Apply for benefits (financial support from the government).

interactiveDots.title: Finding Your Way
interactiveDots.text: Find places to shop, places of worship, schools, parks and public transport in your local area.

interactiveDots.title: Work and English
interactiveDots.text: Register for English language classes and start looking for work. Your support network will help with job applications but cannot give you a job directly.

content.text: There are extensive train, bus and tram services across the UK. Public transport is safe and used by everyone. Tips: buy weekly or monthly tickets, use contactless payment, and take buses rather than trains to save money. You must always pay for your ticket. Not doing so could result in a fine.
Taxis and ride apps (Uber, Bolt) are available but more expensive than public transport. Your support network will help you understand local transport options.
Cycling is popular and affordable. In some areas you can hire bikes. Always wear a helmet, wear bright clothing and use cycle lanes where available.

To drive you need a valid licence, car insurance and a registered car with MOT and vehicle tax. All passengers must wear seat belts. Children need the correct safety seat. Using your phone while driving is a criminal offence. You can use your existing licence for 12 months, then you must pass UK tests. Buying and insuring a car is expensive, public transport is often cheaper.
Your support network will not always be available. During working hours (Monday to Friday) they will be there to help, but outside these hours you may need to manage on your own.
Ask questions whenever you are unsure about something. Tell your support contacts if you have any concerns or worries.
Start learning English as soon as possible as this is the most important step towards independence.
The UK is a multi-faith society. There are mosques, churches, synagogues, temples and other places of worship. You are free to practise your religion.

Your support network will help you find local places of worship. If there is none for your faith nearby, they can help you find a community prayer space and a faith leader. Many resettled people have found support, friendship and community through their place of worship.
Learning and speaking English is key to integration. It will help you find work, support your children’s education, access services, build friendships and become independent more quickly.
Your support network will help you register for English language and literacy classes (ESOL) in your local area.
The British Council offers many free tools and activities to help you learn English:

sections.title: Can My Family Join Me in the UK?

content.text: If you have been resettled without some family members, it is important to understand that resettlement places are very limited globally. The likelihood of additional family members being identified is unfortunately very low.

UK Family Reunion rules allow spouses (if married before arrival) and dependent children under 18 to apply. In exceptional circumstances, others may qualify. There is no guarantee that other family members will be able to join you.

If you find it difficult to be separated from your family, please speak with your support network. They can help you access support services. If family members outside the UK have safety concerns, they should contact their nearest UNHCR office.
